印度桑圖爾琴為梯形擊弦揚琴，屬伊朗桑圖爾變體，傳統於查謨與喀什米爾，可追溯至古代: The Indian santoor is a trapezoid struck dulcimer, a variant of the Iranian santur, traditional to Jammu and Kashmir and traceable to antiquity. Ancient Sanskrit texts call it shatatantri vina (the hundred-string vina). Some researchers place it as an improvised version of a Mesopotamian-period instrument (1600–900 BC). In Kashmir it accompanies folk music and is played in Sufiana Musiqi; Sufi mystics use it to accompany hymns. The Indian version is more rectangular than its Persian counterpart and can carry more strings; the Persian instrument usually has 72 strings, while the Indian one commonly has 25 bridges with four strings each, a hundred in all.

桑圖爾琴（Santoor）是印度傳統擊弦揚琴，為伊朗桑圖爾的變體，屬弦鳴樂器。琴: The santoor is a traditional Indian struck dulcimer, a variant of the Iranian santur, and a chordophone. The body is usually trapezoid with a frame of walnut or maple, wooden bridges on the soundboard, and metal strings strung in groups from side to side, commonly twenty-five bridges with four strings each, a hundred in all. The player sits with the instrument on the knees and strikes it with light wooden hammers, close to or away from the bridges for different timbres, and can damp with the palm. It is used in the folk music of Jammu and Kashmir, in Sufiana Musiqi and to accompany Sufi hymns.
演奏桑圖爾琴時，採半蓮坐姿，將琴置於膝上，寬邊靠近腰、窄邊向外。初學先確認右側調: To play the santoor, sit cross-legged with the instrument on the knees, the wide side towards the waist and the narrow side outward. A beginner should first check that the tuning pins on the right bring each group of strings to the pitch wanted, then take a light wooden hammer in each hand and strike the strings. Striking close to the bridge or a little away from it gives different timbres; while one hand strikes, the other can damp with the palm for variety. The instrument is quiet, so practise with light strokes and slides rather than heavy ones.
金屬弦張於木橋上，以輕木槌敲擊發聲。演奏者以輕擊與滑擊控制發聲，擊點靠近或稍離琴: Metal strings are stretched over wooden bridges and sounded with light wooden hammers. The player controls the sound with light strokes and slides, and striking near the bridge or a little away from it gives different timbres; the other hand can damp with the palm for variety. A typical Indian santoor has two sets of bridges and a range of three octaves. Compared with the Persian santur, the Indian santoor is more rectangular and can carry more strings; the Persian instrument usually has seventy-two strings, while the Indian one commonly has twenty-five bridges with four strings each, a hundred in all.
